svg.text: MPx Sol: Solar Photocatalytic Degrader for Used Filters
A small box solar cooker: a mirror lid and sloped quartz top send sunlight onto a TiO₂-coated tray, where UV makes radicals that oxidise the captured microplastics towards CO₂ and water. Sun only.
A · A box solar cooker for used filters
1 · Mirror lid: bounces extra sun (and UV) in
3 · Air space: traps heat like any box cooker
5 · Particles, washed off the used filter
6 · TiO₂-coated tray on a slide-out drawer
7 · Black liner: turns light into heat
11 · Breather: lets CO₂ out, air in
Ordinary window glass blocks much of the UV, so the top must be quartz or borosilicate.
C · How it breaks plastic down
needs UV below ~390 nm (TiO₂ band gap)
pull off H, add O, the chain breaks
Heat speeds every step. Stopping early leaves
smaller fragments, even nanoplastics, so run
D · Why this doesn't happen on its own
In a river or the sea
Natural weathering mostly breaks plastic into smaller pieces rather than
destroying it; that is how microplastics form in the first place. Shape matters
too: the same plastic lasts under 2 years as a thin film but over 1,400 as a bead [4].
E · How long it takes (log scale)
PS beads on TiO₂ film, UV lamp, lab [1]
LDPE + ZnO rods, visible light, lab [2]
Estimates assume ~6 h of good sun a day and a mirror lid adding 1.5–2× light. Noon sun carries
roughly as much UV-A as a lab lamp, but only for part of the day. Real times must be measured.
BEFORE IT GOES BACK TO NATURE
1 · Run until the tray looks clean.
2 · Test a drop of the residue with MPx Detect
3 · Compost the paper or mycelium filter;
4 · The TiO₂ tray stays in the device for reuse.
Not yet shown in sunlight at this size.
